summary: Count the primes strictly less than n.
mainInsight: Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark all numbers as prime, then for each prime p up to sqrt(n) cross out p*p, p*p + p, ... Starting at p*p is enough because smaller multiples were already crossed by smaller primes.

approaches.name: Trial division per number
approaches.summary: Test each number up to sqrt.

approaches.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
approaches.summary: Cross out multiples of each prime starting at p * p.

commonMistakes: Starting the inner loop at 2p instead of p*p (correct but slower)

promptVariants: Which algorithm counts primes below n fastest in practice?
options: Sieve of Eratosthenes: cross out multiples from each prime's square
Trial division of every number by all the smaller numbers before it
A hash set holding every number that is divisible by two or three
Binary search on the count of primes below each candidate value
cards.answer: Sieve of Eratosthenes: cross out multiples from each prime's square
cards.explanation: The leftover unmarked numbers are exactly the primes.

promptVariants: Why can the inner loop start at p * p and the outer loop stop at sqrt(n)?
cards.answer: A composite number m < n has a prime factor at most sqrt(n). Multiples of p below p * p, such as p * k with k < p, already have the smaller prime factor k (or one of its prime factors) and were crossed out in an earlier round, so crossing can begin at p * p.
cards.explanation: That brings the time to O(n log log n).
Sum of n / p over primes p up to n.

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Space complexity (excluding the input): ___
cards.explanation: A boolean array of size n.
